topic.idea: Qandeel acts after ENEC's early warning. A drift planner predicts if and when a swarm reaches the Barakah intake. A bubble curtain across the 967 metre mouth holds it at sea, a boat closes a floating boom around the held swarm, and tows it away in a closed bag to release it alive. The curtain is one layer; the existing screens stay as the last line.
topic.curtain: Ten 97 metre plastic pipes lie on concrete sleepers 0.75 metres above the seabed. Air leaves 2 millimetre holes and rises, driving a surface current of about 0.45 metres per second out to sea. At the normal setting of 3 litres per second per metre it holds an approach current of about 0.27 metres per second; in 2025 the average was 0.14 and the worst 5 percent was 0.23. Tap a section on the water to switch it off.
topic.blowers: Three oil-free screw blowers in containers on the western tip, two on duty and one on standby, push about 174 cubic metres of air a minute at about 1.1 bar. Air is set hour by hour from the forecast, which uses 29 to 43 percent of the energy of a fixed airflow. A full 72 hour event uses about 31 megawatt-hours, roughly 3,100 US dollars of electricity.
topic.pocket: In our model the intake flow keeps held jellyfish in a dense patch in front of the middle of the curtain. A workboat sweeps that patch with a 200 metre ocean boom with a 66 metre opening and closes a fabric bag around it; in the simulator one sweep collects most of the held swarm. Moored pockets at the breakwater tips stay as a backup.
topic.boats: Workboats of 8 to 10 metres with 1 to 2 tonnes of bollard pull take a closed bag of about 10 tonnes and tow it at 0.2 metres per second, which kept 84 to 100 percent of the jellyfish in our model, to a release point about 3 kilometres north-north-west. Above 1 metre waves they stand by; above 2 metres they shelter and the curtain keeps working alone.
topic.depth: ENEC describes Blue Blubber as dense. The curtain's strong outflow is in a surface layer about one and a half metres deep, which is our assumption. If a swarm averages two to three metres deep, the curtain may hold only about 30 to 80 percent, and the bag still keeps most of what it catches. That is why the sea pilot measures swarm depth first.
topic.plant: Barakah has four 1,400 megawatt units. Each draws up to 172.5 cubic metres of seawater a second through this intake channel and its screens, up to about 690 for the plant (a maximum; no per-unit intake data is used). Through the 967 metre mouth that is roughly 0.08 to 0.1 metres per second toward the intake, which matches the intake draw in our model. Swarms that reach the screens can force the units to reduce power.
topic.site: Everything you see is the real Barakah coast from a Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite image taken on 1 November 2025, at 10 metres per pixel. The breakwaters, the intake channel, the curved outer breakwater and the discharge to the east are real. Jellyfish and boats in this simulator cannot cross them; they must go around, as they would at sea. Water depths are approximate, not a survey.
topic.cost: The lean design costs about 2.3 to 6.5 million US dollars to build, including contingency, and 0.4 to 1 million a year to run. One reactor unit-day of lost output is worth about 1.7 to 2.7 million dollars, so avoiding one to four unit-days repays it. A one-section sea pilot costs about 0.3 to 0.7 million.
mission.0: This is the real Barakah coast, from a Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite image. ENEC's offshore monitoring flags a Blue Blubber swarm, and Qandeel starts here, after the warning. In this demo the swarm starts a few hundred metres from the intake mouth and time runs fast; each bell is one modelled jellyfish, drawn larger from the air so it can be seen.
mission.2: Blowers on the western breakwater send air to ten pipes on the seabed across the 967 metre mouth. At the normal setting, about 174 cubic metres of air a minute at about 1.1 bar, the rising bubbles drive a surface current of about 0.45 metres per second out to sea.
mission.3: This is one section, cut away. Air leaves 2 millimetre holes in a 200 millimetre plastic pipe 0.75 metres above the seabed. The plume turns into an outward current near the surface and jellyfish in that layer are held back. Blue Blubber is dense; if a swarm sits deeper than this layer, more get through, shown in red. The sea pilot measures swarm depth first.
mission.4: The intake flow keeps the held jellyfish in a dense patch in front of the middle of the curtain. A workboat sweeps the patch with a floating boom and closes a fabric bag around it. Moored pockets at the breakwater tips stay as a backup.
mission.5: A workboat of 8 to 10 metres with 1 to 2 tonnes of bollard pull takes a closed fabric bag of about 10 tonnes and tows it at 0.2 metres per second, about seven hours round the outer breakwater, to a release point about 3 kilometres north-north-west, where the jellyfish are released alive. Above 1 metre waves the boats stand by; above 2 metres they shelter and the curtain keeps working.
mission.1: The drift planner releases virtual jellyfish into real 2025 Copernicus currents and ERA5 winds. For an alert 15 kilometres north-north-west it gave a 44 percent chance of arrival within 16 to 73 hours and switched the curtain on 13 hours after the alert.
